utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I ask the Registrar to call out the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-T, Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi and Mr. Vos for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My name is Mr. Toma Fila, I appear with Mr. Petrovic for Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As usual, I will turn to Mr. Dokmanovic to ask him whether he can hear me well -- thank you. Before we start, I have some bad news. I have received from the Registry a note saying that in the week of May starting on 18 May, we cannot afford to sit for more than three hours, namely, from 9 to 12, instead of from 8.30 to 12.30 as we had planned, because the Tribunal cannot pay for a third team of interpreters, so I am afraid we will have less time, but we will try to manage. I understand that the Registry is also offering us another option, namely, instead of sitting every day that week, from 9 to 12, to sit only three days -- two and a half days actually -- and each time, on Monday, Tuesday, the whole day, because then the courtroom will be taken by the other case, Aleksovski, that week. Instead of having five hearings of three hours, we would have two and a half days each -- except for Wednesday, when we would have only half a day -- we would have full days on Monday and Tuesday. I understand probably from the viewpoint of the unit for the protection of victims and witnesses it would be much better. Let us think about that and perhaps we can decide tomorrow. I will be happy to hear from the parties what their preference is. Let us now leave it in abeyance and we move to our next witness. Could you please stand up and make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly swear to the tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing about the truth WITNESS DA

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since this is a witness who requested protective measures including distortion of image and a pseudonym. I hope those measures are in place now. I will now show to the witness a piece of paper with his name and I would ask the witness to confirm whether this is indeed his name and we would like to call this witness under the pseudonym A -- since this is the first Defence witness to have requested this protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it might be confusing if they double up with our pseudonym numbers, if they could select the next alphabetical one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we could call him DA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, something to distinguish him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, DA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would like the usher to show this piece of paper to Witness DA so that the witness can confirm whether this is indeed his name. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document will be marked as D50.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask the witness to state whether, on 16 September 1997, he gave an interview, a statement, to Miroslav Vasic, whether he had signed that statement and whether this is the statement. I tender the statement in Serbian and in the English translation. (Handed). Can you please confirm whether this is your statement and your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D51, English translation D51A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would now like the witness to be shown a statement he gave to the Defence investigator on 26 February -- again, I have the Serbian and English versions and if he can confirm whether this is the statement and whether both the English and Serbian versions have been signed by him.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D52, English translation D52A. D51 and D52 will all be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: There is also the supplement. I would now like to ask the witness whether these are his statements and are they signed by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, both statements have been signed by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The microphone for the witness has not been switched on. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These statements are both mine and the signatures are mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If there are no objections I would like to tender these statements as Defence exhibits under the numbers with which they have been marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you a graduate mechanical engineer and where did you graduate from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I graduated from the Novi Sad faculty -- the faculty of technical sciences, mechanical engineering, I am a graduate mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1987 I lived in Pacetin in the Vukovar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was employed in the Borovo company in the machinery and tools factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you stop coming to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was going to my work until 2 May 1991 -- from May 1991 on I was afraid to go to work any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2 May I was en route from Vukovar to Vinkovci where I was intercepted by the Croatian police, or the army -- they were going by the side of the road, and in a fighting formation they stopped me there. I was with my wife in our car. They approached us, and they put their weapons against our heads, they questioned us what was happening on the road which we had already passed and after a while they allowed us to go on, and that was the reason why I no longer went to Borovo and to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the period that preceded the war, were you involved in political activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not engaged in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You were in the Government of the Serbian district of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem as the Minister for Communications. When were you appointed the Minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the Minister in that Government -- the Government itself was formed in September 1991, and that is when I was appointed to that Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that you were appointed or elected the Minister without having had any previous political experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was elected a Minister according to a different principle or standard, because I had graduated from a technical faculty -- since, as I said, I am a graduate of the technical faculty, that was the reason why I was elected the Minister of Transport and Communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the criterion for the appointment of Ministers in that Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, professional experience in my case, and in most of the cases, maybe some of the Ministers were not elected according to that criterion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how Slavko Dokmanovic was appointed a Minister in the Serbian district Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic was elected according to the same criterion and at the same time. Since Dokmanovic is an agricultural engineer, an agronomist, he was elected the Minister of Agriculture, and in the election process Slavko Dokmanovic had some problems, because in the previous period, before the Government was appointed, he was the President of the Municipal Assembly in Vukovar, and the Serbian population was not happy with him, so his participation was not something that everybody was happy about, but he was elected the Minister of Agriculture of the Serbian district all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was your competence as the Minister of Transport and Communications in the Serbian district Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the very name of the Ministry defines the competence, but in September conditions were a bit specific, and what I could do was also a bit questionable. At the first session of the Government, I proposed that we should not be using the term "Government" at all and that we should not be labelled as Ministers, but officers in charge, since we could only undertake to solve some current problems and according to priorities. This is not something that is in the purview of Ministers. As far as my competency is concerned, I had to solve problems and to achieve that we have at least some telephone communications with the rest of the world, to repair at least some of the roads, and to organise communications -- at least some bus service in the district, because it was cut off from the rest of the world at that time. In my view, this is not something that a Minister should be doing, and the Government, but this is the only thing we could do in the conditions in which we lived in this period from September on. My first task was for this group of people which called itself the Government, because the Government was only appointed -- there were no assistants to Ministers and they could not find personnel, because there were not that many people who were capable of working or who were prepared to accept jobs like that, so we solved those mundane problems for the population that still remained in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Slavko Dokmanovic as the Minister of Agriculture was doing, what were the tasks that he was engaged in at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, since this is September, and since the preparations for the harvest and the sowing were underway, and since there were no production materials left, no machinery left to harvest the crops, he was engaged in that -- since he used to work in Vupic until the beginning of the war, some parts of the Vupic company remained in the areas outside of Vukovar -- Vukovar of course was something else. His task was to coordinate all those cooperatives and companies and to seek assistance. His whole work boiled down to looking for donors and sponsors who would be able to organise something, so that not all the harvest that had -- not all the crops that had to be harvested -- so that at least something of that could be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did the policy of the Government in the district, how was it implemented? Can you please explain what areas composed the Serbian district and then explain how and to what extent the Government policies were implemented in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The district itself was cut off, in practical terms, the eastern or the southern part, with the part of the farmer Vinkovci municipality. There was the Vukovar municipality without the city of Vukovar, and a part of the Osijek municipality -- this is in the Srem and Slavonia part and on the other side of Bosna, there was Baranja. It was very difficult to link this all up and to implement some kind of a policy. I think it took quite some time for the people to get to know the so-called Ministers who were supposed to implement the policies. We were unable to implement any of those policies and to work in the field as far as the political aspect of the job was concerned. The only possibility was for the Ministries vitally linked to certain parts of the economy to organise something, and maybe coordinate something, and it usually depended on your personal contacts and connections, so you could not really define that as implementing a policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: With the part of the district to the south of the town of Vukovar, did you have any access to that territory at all? The decisions of the Government, if we can call it that, were they implemented in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the most difficult area, we had very little or no links at all with that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were they cut off in communication terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were cut off completely, there were no telephone communications, and in order to get from the seat of the Government, which was in Erdut, to that area, you had to travel more than 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Erdut or from Pacetin where I lived, I had to go to Erdut, cross the Danube to Bogunjevo and then go to Backa Palanka and then go through Sid and then back to the area. It was longer than the road to Belgrade -- even further than to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the influence of the Government on the events as a whole in the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the influence of the Government on the events was virtually nil. The Government or the Prime Minister and certain Ministries had some contacts with the international community which was already involved in some way in the events, so those who came from the outside world, from the international community, were not able to communicate with the local communities in the field and if they were unable to communicate with them, then they would contact the Government in Erdut, and we who were in charge of the economy did not take part in the negotiations with the representatives of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was actually the authority -- who carried out the power in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this Government was -- had the ambition to exercise the power in the mandate which was quite short, but it was unable to do so. There were local communities all over this area; there were the village watches, the village headquarters, and in fact in those individual villages they were in charge of functioning of those villages. The Government merely tried to help to put those people in touch with other people who wanted to provide assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The headquarters in the villages, did they receive orders from the Government and, if they did receive those orders, did they comply with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, the Government was unable to issue orders to all those headquarters, so the compliance was non-existent because there were no orders. They mostly dealt, all those Ministers were trying to constitute the Ministries themselves and, also, the services that were associated with Ministries, but they were unable to do so. Some had the ambition to form, for instance in justice and in the judiciary, to make things function in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us now be more specific, what period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am talking about this whole period of the mandate of the Government and that was until the end of January 1992. As far as the Department of Justice is concerned, I know that some of the courts had been established, but I do not want to talk about that in any detail, because I do not know what these courts were and what their jurisdiction was, but I know that they were trying to do something about that. They were trying to gather all the lawyers in the field, and to do something so that at least that branch of the Government would function.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the Minister of Defence and the Minister of the Interior in the Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, all the Ministries were present -- all the Ministries for which we knew, they had all been established, all the Ministers had been appointed -- the Minister of Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the army, did you have the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, neither the army nor the police, we only had the Ministers, but they came to the Government sessions very seldom and they would change very often, after just a few days, because they did not have their competencies defined and that caused problems, so the easiest solution was to remove a person from the office and to appoint another and then to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Government of the Serbian district, did it control any of the armed formations in the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, we did not even have reports about what was happening in some parts of the region, as far as these armed formations were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The members of the Government, did they belong to an armed unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can speak for myself as a member of the Government -- I did not belong to any of the units and if my mandate expired, then I was a member of the Territorial Defence in my village, in the place where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was it the same with Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the same applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did members of the Government carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them were not armed. I never carried any weapons. Some of the members of the Government had their security details, but most of them not. I think that maybe even the Prime Minister had his security, the rest of us we did not have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it would be a good time now to explain how the Government of the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem was formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Government was formed and appointed by the Assembly of the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem -- of course by voting, by ballot at the proposal of the mandate, he became the Prime Minister of course and then he proposed the Ministers, who were appointed and I do not know at what date, but it was in September, by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is the Great National Assembly, who composed this Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Great National Assembly was composed of the Assemblymen from the Assemblies of the municipalities, which were under the control of the Serbian district, and who were in the field, that is to say, in the district, and, also, a large number of people who were put forward by the local communities in the region, and they were also co-opted into that Assembly. According to some kind of a key, depending on the size of the settlement, those people from the local communities were also recruited into the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many members there were in the Great National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number but I think it is close to 200 but I am not sure about that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is the Serbian National Council for the Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian National Council -- and I am now talking on the basis of a rumour, on the basis of what I heard -- it was formed in early 1990 -- myself and most of the people did not know who was in the National Council. The reason why it was formed was to protect Serbian interests in the district. Before the Government was formed, we learned who were some of the people who were members of that council, and after that it was no longer -- it did not exist any more, because there was a Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This National Council, was it a legitimate representative of the Serbian population in that area? Was it democratically elected or appointed in any other democratic manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not formed according to a ballot or an election; it was for a while even a secret -- some kind of a secret society. Since I was not in that Council, I do not know what was the criterion for the election into that Council, but they simply started to issue proclamations as tensions rose in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Slavko Dokmanovic a member of the Serbian National Council for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, on the basis of my knowledge from August and September, he was not a member of the Serbian National Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that another Serbian National Council existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about the Serbian National Council of Serbs in 1990. There were reports in the press about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So there was the Serbian National Council with a seat in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether it was in Knin or in the village of Srb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was it formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1990, in July or August -- I am not sure about the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the role of Mr. Dokmanovic in that National Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know what the atmosphere was and what the opinion of Dokmanovic was at the time, and this all has to do with the National Council. I know that Dokmanovic was in Srb as the President of the Vukovar Municipal Assembly, and most of the Presidents of the municipalities with the Serbian majority were invited there, and it was published that Dokmanovic was also a member of that Council -- there were reports in the press -- it was not a secret. But things developed in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What were the reactions to that news?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among the Serbian population, there were not any particular reactions, but the Croatian population, or, rather, the HDZ as the Party in power, reacted very strictly to all that, and very soon Slavko Dokmanovic left that National Council -- it all probably happened within a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it all happened in 1990 before the autumn of 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that is when the Serbs began to react, and they criticised Dokmanovic for leaving and it was interpreted as giving way to the HDZ, which, regardless of the fact in Vukovar, in the Assembly, it was not a majority Party, but it was slowly beginning to take over power, and it appeared that he was very tolerant towards the minority in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us return to the Serbian National Council for the district of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, that second Serbian National Council, which existed in the region in which you worked. Were there any links between that Council and the Great National Council and the Government of the Serbian district itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not see any links there in the political sense. I do not know if there was continuity of any kind, but only some individuals from that Council became members of the Great National Assembly, deputies there, and some of these individuals were members of the Government of the Serbian district.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long have you known Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have known Slavko Dokmanovic for a long time -- more than 20 years. I know him as a man who played football in the local club, first of all, and it was the opposite team to the one in my particular locality. I know he came to my village, because he had relations there and that is how we met. We were officially introduced at the beginning of September 1991, and I met him personally on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You are from Pacetin. What were the opinions in Pacetin of Dokmanovic while he was performing his function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the general view was not a favourable one -- he was not regarded as being a good President, because of his tendency to give way. There were other matters, too, that he was criticised for, for example, for allowing SUP to go from Vukovar to Vinkovci and similar things -- some of these things were actually not true, but the tension was such between the Serbs and the Croats that the Serbs did not have much confidence in him. They did not have a very good opinion of Slavko Dokmanovic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where is Pacetin located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pacetin -- if you go from Vukovar towards Vinkovci, it is halfway between the two. You turn right on this road -- I do not know how clear I can make it -- it is in a triangle between Osijek, Vinkovci and Vukovar and it is equidistant from these three towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the time when war operations were being waged in the area, what were the living conditions in Pacetin and its environs -- Bobota, for example, or Erdut, which is -- Trpinja, which are fairly near?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in all these places, at least the ones that I moved around in, that the living conditions were more or less similar -- they were all difficult -- the whole region was left without electricity, which meant that there was no water, no telephone communication, and life changed overnight. There was no problem with food in that region, because it is a rich agricultural region, but everything else created great problems. There was no communication, there were no buses, bus routes. So, the living conditions were difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did Slavko Dokmanovic come to work most frequently -- I suppose you saw him in the Government building in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did see him frequently, and I remember him coming to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in a sort of fashionable type of suit, a dark grey hunting suit. In the summer period, he would be just wearing a sort of vest, but when it was colder, he would have a shirt, dark green in colour with brown. That is what I saw him wearing most often.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me now move to the period which is the most interesting for all of us here, that is to say, the end of November 1991. At the Government meeting of 19 November 1991, was it decided that the members of the Government should meet the following day in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at a document, please, which the usher is going to show you, and tell us what the document relates to. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D53 and the French translation D53A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the minutes from a Government meeting held on 19 November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the introductory part, please tell me whether you took part in the meeting? Is your name and your presence recorded there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is -- my name is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you read out point 3 on page 2 of the minutes -- the last paragraph on that page on page 2, above the signature of the recorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Goran Hadzic, President of the Government, informed the members that, due to the situation, it was necessary for the Government members to come on Wednesday, 20 November 1991, to Vukovar and for Friday 22 November 1991, a meeting of the Government is convened in Beli Manastir for 9 o'clock."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I tender this in evidence as Defence exhibit number 53 and the French translation 53A, if there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, although it is only in Serbian and French; you do not mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I understand French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We have it in English as well, if you need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We can tender that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The English translation will be D53B.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You read out a moment ago the last paragraph of the minutes, where it states that it is necessary for the members of the Government to go to Vukovar on Wednesday. Can you tell us whether it was a Government meeting, or a meeting of the members of the Government and what the difference is between those two concepts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a meeting of the Government at which an agenda was to be formed and minutes kept in the form of the document that you have just shown me. It was a meeting of the members of the Government, because the Government did not have any links with Vukovar as a town, and there were intimations that there would be a settling of accounts with members of the Government, because those who were in Vukovar did not accept the existence of a Government and the formation of a Government and that a Government can decide on any matters at all, so that it was an affirmative, an assertive meeting, so to speak, to show that there was some form of Government, that the name given was a sort of form of organisation and that these divisions should stop. It was not an easy thing to go to Vukovar at the time, and the dilemma remained as to who would be going to Vukovar, which Government members, and that is why the Government did not convene the meeting but it was just a meeting of the members of the Government to show that some form of Government existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When were the members of the Government to meet in Vukovar and was the locality discussed as to where the meeting would be convened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not discuss the venue, but when entering into Negoslavci there are only several locations where this meeting could take place, where all these people could get together and one of those venues was the municipal -- the administrative building that is to say, and the building of VELEPROMET in Vukovar -- the VELEPROMET company and it was decided to come sometime around noon or after 12, and that the meeting itself would take place at around 2 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the atmosphere in the VELEPROMET building -- the VELEPROMET company's building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many people there, a mass of people, and we did not know where they all came from. Some of them came up from the cellars, civilians, there were members of the territorial units of the army. It was even difficult to enter the yard of the compound itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May we now see a videotape, which we are all well acquainted with, and I should like the witness to tell us whether the tape depicts what he saw that day in the VELEPROMET area. Is that the atmosphere that prevailed and are those the people who were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the clothing worn by Slavko Dokmanovic; was that the usual kind of clothing that he wore at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we see this tape in colour, please? The tape is in colour, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise anybody on that tape -- did that happen on that day and in that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is VELEPROMET. I do know some of the people there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us some of their names -- who did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised Goran Hadzic, Slavko Dokmanovic. I know the voice of Rade Leskovac, I recognised his voice, and Zladko Kosic and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see what Slavko Dokmanovic was wearing? Was that the usual type of clothing that he was wearing when you had occasion to see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see the colour -- it appeared to be that type of clothing, but I did not see the colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May we have the tape shown in colour, because it does exist in colour. We saw the tape yesterday, the Defence and myself and it was in colour -- it was a colour tape.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It appears that there is some technical problem. THE BOOTH: The only copy we got was black and white. There is no colour copy here available.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask the witness to be shown Defence Exhibit 48 -- it refers to the clothing. Is that the clothing that Slavko Dokmanovic wore at the time? It is D48 and that is the clothing itself. (Handed). Take a look at the clothing, please -- take it out of the bag. You can take it out of the plastic bag and tell us whether that is the clothing in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that all this took place, the meeting we are talking about, took place on 20 November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, because for the first time after 2 May I was in Vukovar, on the occasion, and what I saw there can never be forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you see in that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that mass of people that had gathered there, people who had been having a hard time. As I came before 2 o'clock, I walked around VELEPROMET, some 100 metres around VELEPROMET, and the devastation and the rubble and the dead people -- dead bodies about the town is something that one can only see -- that you cannot describe. It is a terrible impression -- the scenes that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see dead people, people killed of the Serb nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know, if I see somebody lying down, whether they are Serbs or Croats, but there were a lot of them at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you arrive in Vukovar -- what road did you take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to Vukovar from Erdut to Palanka via Sid and then further on to Tovarnik, Orolik and there the road moves on to Negoslavci and I entered Vukovar via Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any control points along the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were several control points, which -- and you had to show your documents at each of these checkpoints and you needed permits to go to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who issued these permits and what did they allow you to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They allowed movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who were they issued by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military authorities issued these permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that, in the area that we are discussing, military administration existed at the time on 20 November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we got these permits in Erdut from someone -- I do not exactly know what service issued those permits. I just received them. I did not ask for them personally -- asked to be granted these permits personally. It was done by the secretary of the Government, or some such official. Although we did have our official IDs, which allowed us movement, but in that case, those IDs were not sufficient -- we had to have these additional permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the VELEPROMET building. Why did the members of the Government meet at VELEPROMET itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a mass of people inside and we found ourselves there, too. Everybody coming out of the town came to this VELEPROMET compound and that is where we found ourselves. We did not know where we would actually hold this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was it the only place where people could meet in view of the fact that the town had been almost completely destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was a risky business going further away from the VELEPROMET compound, because there were a lot of mines, and of the buildings that existed we had the Vinarija building, but there was nobody in that building -- everybody was in the VELEPROMET compound and it was logical for all of us to meet up there. At that particular point, you could not plan where you would be holding a possible meeting, because, at least when I came, we began to meet people we knew, relatives, and there were no conditions -- proper conditions for holding a Government meeting of an official kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was decided for the Government members to meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, they were to arrive a little earlier, but the meeting was to have taken place at 2 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did the meeting start and where was it held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting started a little after 2 p.m. -- I do not know exactly what time -- and it was held in the administrative building of the VELEPROMET company -- when you enter the courtyard, on the right-hand side there is a building, you go into the corridor in the first or second door on the right and there was a corridor -- a hall -- where the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long did the meeting last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It lasted for about an hour, more or less. I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember some of the people who were there. I remember that the Prime Minister was there and the President of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us their names please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ilija Koncarevic was there, Goran Hadzic was there, Mladen Hadzic was there, Vitomir Devetak, Bogdan Vojnovic, Slavko Dokmanovic, Boro Bogunovic and some others I do not know. I am certain about the ones I have mentioned -- the others I cannot quite recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a set agenda and were minutes kept of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no set agenda, and, as far as I know, there were no minutes, because there were Government meetings later on and minutes would have appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, all the members were highly disturbed and were troubled by what they had seen and we spoke of our impressions and, as it was a meeting of part of the Government, in a way, we tried, as Ministers in this newly arisen situation, when nothing had happened with our arrival in the VELEPROMET compound -- there were no incidents that took place -- so that we can say that Vukovar should be under the control of the Government and the capital of the Serbian district, and some of the Ministers talked about the tasks to be performed by each of us in our particular departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was the area that we are talking about under military rule at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army was present, but the manner in which it was present, I do not know -- the kind of control it had, I do not know. There were people coming in, in military uniforms -- I do not know their names. One of them said he was the commander of the town and he said that the town was under his competencies and that the Government had nothing to do there -- nothing to undertake, nor was it necessary for it to be present in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Slavko Dokmanovic attended the meeting and whether he was in the hall where the meeting took place all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was at the meeting and, during that one hour, while the meeting lasted, he was inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he take part in the discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and he spoke about his department, that is to say, agriculture, and what remained to be done in view of the newly arisen situation and, as this district of Srem was not divided any more, but was conjoined, he spoke about the final harvest and the sowing season and that was the 19th and 20th of November. He said what had been completed and what was still to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave the VELEPROMET compound and where did you go -- in what direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left soon after the end of the meeting -- perhaps I stayed on for five more minutes. Some other people left the building with me, who had come out of the cellars -- perhaps five or 10 minutes later I took the same road towards Negoslavci, through Negoslavci, Orolik and back to Sid and the same way I had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you stopped along the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the checkpoints were the same ones as when we came, three or four. One I recall vividly, at the entrance to Olijek -- that was the largest checkpoint. After that, there were checkpoints, but they were not as stringent as the checkpoint that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us who managed the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was it the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is how I saw it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, have you finished your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution would request a brief recess for cross-examination of this witness. The prior statement that we had made no mention whatsoever that this individual was in the Government. It just indicated that -- it is very brief, I think your Honours have it, and he says that Slavko Dokmanovic was President of the Municipal Assembly from Vukovar and talks about that and then he goes: "I know that 10 days after the liberation of Vukovar the Executive Council of the municipality set up its first form of civilian rule." The first time we found out he was a member of the Government was when we received this statement this morning, or that he was present at the meeting at VELEPROMET. Therefore we request some time before we commence cross-examination on this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I grant your request. I think we could maybe have a recess until 10 o'clock -- is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour. How about five after -- if we could have 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, 5 minutes after 10. We will stand adjourned now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: First of all I would like to thank you, your Honours, for your indulgence for the 30-minute recess. Witness DA, you talk about this Serb National Council and you have indicated in your testimony, I believe, that Slavko Dokmanovic attended these meetings in Srb, which is near Knin, in his role as President of the Vukovar municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there as the President of the Vukovar Municipal Assembly in 1990 at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you know anywhere in the statute of the Vukovar municipality where it indicates that these are part of the duties of the President of the municipality, to participate in functions of the Serb National Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know anything about that, because I was not in the Municipal Assembly and I was not involved in politics at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But Vukovar municipality was a multi-ethnic community, was it not -- it was not just made up of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a multi-ethnic community, but with a Serbian majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You think that there was a Serbian majority in Vukovar, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the statistical data indicates that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 188, please. (Handed). Witness DA, if you can look under the figures for Vukovar, which appear on lines 25, 26 and 27, and then percentages on 28, 29 and 30, look for the years 1991, 1981 and 1971 and tell me if, during any of those years, there were more Serbs listed than there were Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Pause). Well, if you look at the figures here, in the absolute figures for Serbs and Croats, if this information is correct, indeed, there are more Croats, but you also have about 6,000 Yugoslavs and Croats -- 6,124 Yugoslavs -- Croats never declared themselves Yugoslavs, only Serbs did that, and also in the Vukovar Municipal Assembly SDP was in the majority and only Serbs voted for them. Slavko Dokmanovic could not have been elected President of the Municipal Assembly in 1990 if Serbs had not won the elections in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Let us take your answer one point at a time. You indicate that only Serbs declared themselves as Yugoslavs. Would you read out the figure of Yugoslavs in the year 1971 for Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please bear in mind that this witness is not an expert for statistics and he cannot give his opinion about statistical data, so I would like the Prosecutor to go on to his next question, if the court sustains the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor is not asking for a sort of technical assessment or scientific assessment from the viewpoint of statistics. He is simply asking the witness to read out the figures which are set out in that particular document. I think it is quite proper -- the Prosecutor may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Would you read out the number of Yugoslavs which are listed in Vukovar municipality in 1971?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What column is that for 71 -- is it column 30?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It is line 27, all the way across under the category of "Yugoslavs", does it not say 4,699 Yugoslavs, for Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Then, for 1981, it shows 17,199 Yugoslavs; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And then, for 1991, 6,124 Yugoslavs; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, let us go back and look on line 27 at the number of Croats in 1971. Does it not show 34,629?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In 1981, it shows 30,157, does it not, so there is a decrease of 4,000 Croats during that period, between 1971 and 1981, is there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that there is a decrease from 34,000 to 30,000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So a decrease of about 4,000. Then, if you look at the figure for the number of Serbs in 1971, it shows 28,470 and the figure of Serbs in 1981 is 25,146, is it not? So it is a decrease of around 3,000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If you would look at the very first figures for 1971 and 1981 which give the total population of Vukovar municipality, it shows an increase in population of 5,000, does it not, from 76,000 to 81,000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is what it says in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So, if you have a decrease of 4,000 Croats and a decrease of 3,000 Serbs, but the continual population of the district grows, and the number of Yugoslavs grow by 12,000, would it not seem to indicate that those 4,000 Croats had also declared themselves as Yugoslavs and, in fact, more Croats had declared themselves as Yugoslavs than Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How can we indulge in such speculation from statistical data, how people declared themselves? These figures do not indicate how the population moved and how the population swung from Serbian and Croatian into Yugoslav. You cannot see this from this data. I would like this to stop, because this is a question for an expert in demographics, not for the fact witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness said that all Yugoslavs were Serbs and he said that no Croats declared themselves as Yugoslavs and he said the statistics will show that. He is the one that said this -- I am testing what he has offered -- the opinion that this witness has offered. If he could offer another explanation after he has said that the statistics show it, for why you have a continual rise in the population, a decrease in the number of Croats, a decrease in the number of Serbs and a rise in the number of Yugoslavs, I am happy to hear it, but he is the one that offered this opinion, and if he is going to say that and he asserts that the statistics show it he should be able to look at the statistics and tell me where they show it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could answer the question and then we move on to a different question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not want to start analysing figures which appear here and they can be interpreted in mathematical terms in different ways, just as the Prosecutor has done. I could have a mathematical model and then state that my theory is true on the basis of this information presented here, but to cut a long story short, I would not now want to use those mathematical models. I just want to state what we all know, Slavko Dokmanovic was the President of the Vukovar Municipal Assembly. One thing is for sure, he was not elected to that position by Croats, and the breakdown of the overall number of the members of the Assembly, they had -- the majority were Serbs, so it was his own assessment whether he can answer the invitation and to attend the session of the Serb National Council. I think that we have to simply cut this whole thing short, because otherwise we will not be able to extricate ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You said that his involvement with the Serb National Council occurred in the autumn of 1990; correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be more exact -- which Serb National Council. We keep talking about two Serb National Councils, so please ask this witness a question which will not confuse him right from the start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, may I ask the Prosecutor to clarify this particular point?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated that he participated in the Serb National Council of Knin, or of Srb in autumn of 1990; correct, and that his involvement lasted for perhaps one month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that Slavko Dokmanovic -- this is something that I know from the papers -- that he attended the meeting of Serbs near Knin in Srb in July or August, I cannot remember the exact date, in his capacity as the President of the Municipal Assembly and the reports in the papers were that the Serbian National Council was formed there. I do not know -- I did not read any decisions where it was established and so forth, but I know that after that there was a lot of disturbance among the Croats because he was present there -- after maybe about a month, maybe 25 or 30 days, Slavko no longer participated in the work of the Serbian National Council in Srb and Serbs were not happy with that decision, because he no longer participated in their work. This was again reported in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So this was reported in the papers -- this was known publicly, that he no longer participated in this group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was published in the papers, that he was not there any more. As for how credible all this information is, then the same goes for the two reports -- the first and the second one. I did not participate in the work of that body, so I did not see any decisions or minutes from the meetings. One thing is for sure, that all the Serbs knew that he no longer participated in the work of the Serbian National Council and it was resented in this region, in Vukovar region.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 196 and on page 40 -- we have prepared a draft translation of this portion of this -- this has still not been proof-read. I will provide it to the court for your assistance as we go through this. However, I would ask the court's indulgence to supplement it with a final copy after the Registrar's revisions have been made. The interpreters have already been provided with copies of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for getting involved, but could this practice of translations being promised for a later date be stopped? I still have not received the translation of the law on citizenship which has been promised to me and to this court. Could the Prosecutor's Office put in an effort, just as the Defence team is doing, and we have only two people here, to provide the translations instead of always promising to provide translations. Because if you are talking about a fair trial in which you have one counsel on one side and another one, so two counsel on one side and God knows how many counsel on the other side, then it is probably harder for me to provide translations, so this is an official protest that I am lodging now. This is not something that happens in the Anglo-Saxon law system and in the civil law system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before asking the Prosecutor to reply, may I say that this is not a practice in the common law system and so on, because normally there is only one language so you do not need a translation. To the best of my knowledge, translations are not provided by the Prosecutor's Office but by the Registry, and I may be wrong --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct. Although there are four of us sitting at this table, none of us speak Serbo-Croatian, although two of his colleagues do, so we are in a position of having to depend entirely on the translators. The fact that there is four of us here does not speed up the process, that the translators are doing the translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us clear this up. This book was tendered by the witness Milenkovic in February 1997 when Slavko Dokmanovic was still at large. Now we are in March/April 1998. If they had wanted to have it translated, they would have done so. This morning I did not want to react before the half hour recess. They received the supplementary statement earlier -- not this morning, the statement that indicates there was a session of the Government in Erdut and they asked for 20 minutes to prepare themselves, but this is something that I was prepared to accept. They have had this book since February 1997, and that is the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If I could reply to that, we did not receive that statement before this morning. That is the first time we have seen the supplemental statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I am sure the Registry will endeavour to provide translations as soon as possible. On the other hand, you must, Mr. Fila, understand and appreciate the difficulties of the Registry, because, in particular, the unit for translation is flooded with documents to be translated. I promise that we will -- I will ask personally the head of the translation unit to make an effort and I am sure that the Prosecutor's Office is also going to cooperate, as it has done so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Certainly, from our own personal perspective, we are unable to operate as attorneys until we have translations. It is certainly in our interests to get it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let us now move on, otherwise we waste our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Witness DA, at the beginning of paragraph 5, or section 5, which appears on page 40, could you read this initial paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Immediately after the council was established, General Dusan Pekic reacted from Belgrade and asked whether it was a 'parallel' for the Council in Knin. On the last day of January 1991, on the premises of the Association of Serbs in Belgrade, on the proposal of Pekic, representatives of the Serbian National Council of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem met with Dr. Milan Babic in order to eliminate all possible dilemmas about the competencies of the two Councils. The following people attended the meeting: Mihailo Vucinic, the President of the Association, Dusan Pekic, Milan Babic, Ilija Koncarevic, Goran Hadzic, Ilija Petrovic, Caslav Ocic and Slavko Dokmanovic. The latter two are not members of the Council." Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "However, Dokmanovic still considers himself a member of the Knin Council despite the fact that he withdrew from it 'because of the public'. Veljko Dzakula from Pakrac was also called to attend the meeting but , as Vucinic said, he refused to come in order to avoid meeting with Ilija Sasic, a lawyer from Podravska Slatina and one of the leaders of the SDS in Slavonia."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You can stop at that point, that is fine. If you would begin reading the third paragraph which is in that section which begins with "Pekic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Pekic tried to moderate Babic's stance and asked him to be more tolerant towards the Council established in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. It was already noticed that the Serbian movement in Croatia was not well coordinated and that many ideas and many actions, as well as the readiness of many people to be active, had been ineffective. It was also noticed that the SDS, which was at the moment the leading light of the Serbian people in Croatia, and the Serbian National Council in Knin lacked men who could coordinate all the activities in all the parts of the country populated by Serbs. Because of that, the Council in established Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem should be supported and that many activities in this area could be completed through it. The Council could also be used for the liberation of the left bank of the Danube River which could then offer assistance, and thus prevent the extermination of the Serbian people on the other side. Babic opposed both Pekic and the participants' arguments, but in the end 'had mercy' and agreed that the said organ should work as a regional committee of the Serbian National Council. This way, said he, many dilemmas and disagreements about the composition and the competencies of the Council could be eliminated. Ocic proposed that instead of the name 'Council' the expression 'Committee' be used, but Babic turned it down and explained that the Statute did not provide for 'the committee'. He continued insisting on 'the Council' being a 'verified name'. Babic then raised his voice and started speaking as if he were superior; he would have difficulties if he, God forbid, would need to share the power he gained. It was probably the result of the situation in Knin, where, as he himself had said, and as Pekic had further explained, there were not enough people who could do serious political work. With his speech he made the impression that he alone represented the Serbian National Council of Krajina, worked on its behalf, made decisions on his own, and probably did not consult with the others much. After a long argument about 'the Council' and 'the committee' and after an unpropitious moment Dokmanovic started insisting on the differences between Vukovar and Knin, Babic finally 'accepted' that the Serbian National Council of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem be renamed the Regional Committee of the Serbian National Council."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is fine, you can stop at that point. Perhaps if the usher could bring the book back, we will have him read one other portion, but if that can be marked, that would make it shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What sort of document is this. Is it minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This is from the same book. This is the history of the Serb National Council which was a book that was prepared -- it was handed over by Mr. Milenkovic. This is one provision -- this is the same page where Mr. Fila had Mr. Milenkovic read the footnote from the other day. We have taken this whole section and have had this draft translation done and would have the final translation supplemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume therefore the author of this text is Petrovic, the author of the whole book?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct. If you can start reading from this point, perhaps the usher can -- starting right there. (Handed). Your Honours, on the translation, this would be at the end of line 2 on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we have this working document -- the draft translation, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If you can begin reading at that point, Witness DA, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Slavko Dokmanovic, an agricultural engineer, until the war -- "

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This has already been read -- if the usher can bring it back again, I will point to the exact spot and do not read the footnotes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Babic assessed that as such Krajina should involve Beli Manastir, municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also asked with certain reserve what would have been a reaction to his proposal that Vukovar be involved in Krajina as well. Both Hadzic and Dokmanovic doubted that such a proposal would be adopted in Vukovar, mostly because Vukovar inclined towards uniting with Vojvodina."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is fine. We would introduce this as the next Prosecutor's exhibit -- this is a translation of just one portion from the entire book, which has already been tendered, so perhaps it would be better to introduce it as Prosecutor's Exhibit 196A because it is just a translation of a document that is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I see -- I apologise -- I see no reason for these excerpts from the book to be treated separately as evidence, if we have already accepted the whole book as D196. Why should we pinpoint these excerpts and admit them once again as separate evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Why not? Is there any problem? It may be useful to have them as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If something has been adopted once, is its value greater if you adopt it five more times? If that is so, then I am going to tender evidence four or five times in the future, if it will have greater value.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is why I suggested it should perhaps be marked as 196A, because it is just a translation of a document already in evidence. I was trying to address that issue before they stood up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Therefore, the only document which is now tendered in evidence is the English translation, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see no objection on the part of Mr. Fila, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Witness DA, can you tell me why was it necessary to have a separate Serb Government in this region -- in the Vukovar region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that, because I did not take part in all this. I have partially read this book and I have my opinion of it -- the portion that I read -- but, as I say, I did not take part in the National Council and in the political events. I said previously that I have information from what was published in the press, so I can go back to the witness, to Slavko Dokmanovic, and September 1991, when his failure to take part in what happened by the Serb public was criticised, and I did not take part in this, nor can I say whether what Ilija Petrovic has written is correct or not. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I did not ask you about what is referred to in the book. I am asking you, in your role as a Minister in this Government, you had to have known the basis for forming the Government in the first place. Why was the Government formed in that region -- what was the reason for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Government was formed by the Assembly of the Serb district in September 1991 and the Government has no continuity with the Serbian National Council. I said that just some people appeared in the Government -- the Prime Minister, Goran Hadzic, for example, was in the Assembly, and, it was also well-known, Koncarevic and Petrovic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The witness thinks you are asking him about the book. Explain to the witness you are not talking about the book but the reasons in general for which a Government was set up in the area, not as explained by Ilija Petrovic in the book, but the real reasons for forming that Government in that area, Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If you want to clarify once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have tried to do that twice, your Honour, but I will try. Mr. DA, why was the Government formed -- putting aside the Serb National Council, putting aside the book, why was the Government formed? What was the reason for forming a Serbian Government for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem -- not how, but why -- what was the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that, there was the setting up of the Assembly of the Serbian district. The reasons probably were that this area in which Serbs lived be united, because the area was made up of parts of the Vinkovci municipality, Osijek, and the municipality of Vukovar. So, all this made up one region, one area at the time, and I am talking on behalf of the Assembly -- it was seen that this district should be conjoined and to set up executive power and authority in the region, because the Assemblies no longer functioned in these areas, particularly the Vinkovci and Osijek municipalities. I cannot -- they proposed that I be in the Government of that Serbian district several days prior to its formation. I could have accepted or rejected the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would like for the witness to be shown Defence Exhibit 19, please, at this time. (Handed). Concurrently with this, the English translation, which is listed as Defence Exhibit 19A. Witness DA, would you look at article 11 of this document, which sets out the areas which are included under the Serbian district and would you tell me, under paragraph 3, for Vinkovci, or section 3 of article 11, it lists all of the communities in Vinkovci municipality, does it not, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The copy is a little dark, but I can see that a lot of the places are enumerated in all the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And it includes the city of Vinkovci, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if it includes the town of Vinkovci -- if they are some places around Vinkovci, then it would be logical to suppose that it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If you look under section 3, I think it appears that it is the second to last name in that section, is it not -- the name of the town of Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And then under section 5 for Osijek, where it says, "Provisional seat in Tenja", it also lists the towns and cities in Osijek municipality, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And, in the centre of that list, it includes the city of Osijek; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And neither Osijek nor Vinkovci were under the control of this Serbian district, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Both Osijek and Vinkovci had sizeable Croatian majorities, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you participate in the discussions where these communities were included within the Serbian district, in your role in the Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never took part in those talks, and it had nothing to do with the Ministry for Communications, so these kind of things did not go through the Ministry. Decisions were taken -- I do not remember when a decision of this kind was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How many Ministers were there in the Government of this Serbian district?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 15 -- I do not know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You have already mentioned some of the different roles -- an Agriculture Minister, a Minister of Interior, a Minister of Defence, a Minister of Agriculture -- was there also a Foreign Minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And who held that post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, Caslav Ocic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remained in the Government from September to the end of January or the beginning of February 1992, so between 1991 and 1992, when the Government ceased to exist in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At that time, it became part of the Republic of Serb Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On the day of this meeting at VELEPROMET -- I am sorry, let me go back -- strike that question. On 19th, you indicated that you attended a meeting in Erdut; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And how many people were present at this meeting in Erdut, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall. There was part of the Government there, and some other people -- I do not know them all. That was a frequent practice, that at Government meetings many other people would attend whom the Ministers did not know -- at least not know all of them, so that I could not tell you what Ministers or anybody else -- it was a long time ago. I could perhaps recall this on the basis of the minutes, but not all the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But Mr. Dokmanovic was present and Mr. Hadzic was present and you were present; correct -- you do remember those three?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as Dokmanovic goes, I do not recall, but Hadzic did, because he presided.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At all events, Slavko was in Erdut. At the meeting, I remembered clearly that it was decided that members of the Government go to Vukovar on the following day. I cannot remember the other things that were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you indicated that, when you went to Vukovar the next day, it made quite an impression on you; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that this was perhaps the most memorable day of your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether it was the most memorable -- I have had better days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am sure. Perhaps that was not a good way to phrase that. But, in any event, it struck your consciousness and your memory very strongly -- everything that you did and everything that happened on that day, I can imagine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That has remained in my memory -- clearly embedded. It is the first time I went to Vukovar after 2 May, to a Vukovar of the type that I saw on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you recall exactly what time you arrived at VELEPROMET, or approximately what time you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know roughly that I arrived somewhere around 12 -- perhaps a little after 12 -- half an hour after 12, and I went a little further off from VELEPROMET to see that part of town, about 100 metres further off, as far as I had the courage to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was that in the direction back towards the town of Vukovar or in the direction towards Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So that would have been very close to the JNA barracks, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The barracks were across the road, if you look at VELEPROMET, so further off from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you go to the JNA barracks at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On this video that we have seen, Defence Exhibit 2, Arkan features very prominently in that. What was his role at the VELEPROMET on that day, 20 November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, Arkan, with perhaps some other individuals -- I do not know the others by sight -- he came with Hadzic as security, in view of the fact that Hadzic did not feel safe coming to Vukovar -- whether that was his security or anything else, he was there with Hadzic.
