utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And approximately what time did this meeting start that everyone was involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting started about 2 or quarter past 2 -- I do not know exactly. It was not before 2; it was a little after 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I believe you indicated in your examination-in-chief that it lasted approximately one hour; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, that is my assessment, it lasted somewhere around one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was it your recollection that everyone who was involved in the meeting stayed inside the meeting room for the entire period, or did some people come and go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some comings and goings but the Ministers who were there did not leave the room -- at least, I do not recall any of the Ministers having left the room, and going in and out of the meeting, but, in the general melee, there were some other people that I do not know and they would walk about and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was there any discussion at this Government meeting or any vote taken as to what was going to be done with the Croatian men who had been taken from the hospital and who were being held at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not discuss that. I did not know that anybody had been taken from the hospital and that he was at some locality or other. It was not information known to the Government, that such a thing had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was there any discussion to the effect that the civilian authorities would take over Croatian war criminals from the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information was given that all these people from VELEPROMET, which included Serbs and Croats -- they were all inside -- that, by military truck, be taken towards the border between Serbia and Croatia -- somewhere around Sid, and that they could then decide where they would be going, whereas taking them over -- there was nobody over there to take them over from the Government. There was nobody to do this, and so we could not discuss this, and for many of them we did not know what was happening, because we came there on that particular day -- some had come immediately prior to the meeting; I had come perhaps an hour before the meeting. I walked around that part of the town and went back to VELEPROMET, because I knew many of the people in the VELEPROMET compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But there was no discussion about prosecuting or gaoling people who were seen as war criminals from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In that part, there was no discussion of this kind, as the commander of the town was decisive and clear, and stated that the Government had nothing to discuss, even questions of the economy, because he is the commander of the town and the town was being controlled by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: There was no discussion about establishing a people's court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Had any of the subjects been discussed in the meeting at Erdut the previous day, on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- at least I do not remember that anything of this kind had been discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me make one thing clear: the Ministry of Justice in the two months had some jobs to do in setting up civilian courts -- not people's courts -- they are regional or district courts or whatever in the hierarchy of courtrooms, but not a people's court -- I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you discuss what had gone on in the meeting with anyone who was outside, after the meeting was concluded -- with anyone who had not been a participant in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean me personally, did I talk to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only talked to the people that I happened to meet by chance in VELEPROMET -- the ones I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have just one question, that is to say a clarification. The exhibit presented to the witness, D19, is a law on territorial and economic organisation and could he clarify as to who adopts the law -- the Government or the Assembly, because, from the answer, one could conclude that it was something adopted by the Government. Therefore, the question is: who adopted the laws in the Serbian district, including that particular law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Laws and this particular law, you can see this from the text, was enacted by the Great National Assembly and it was put forward -- it need not have been put forward by the Government. One of the Ministries, perhaps, or one of the Assembly Councils.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have a few questions. First of all, can you remember the name of the Defence Minister in that particular period, say November 1991 -- who was the Defence Minister of that Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot quite remember who it was at the time. They changed and did not attend the Government meetings much. I think that the first was Ilija Kojic, but later on he was replaced and somebody was appointed and very often nobody was appointed. I cannot quite remember whether at that particular time anybody was appointed as Defence Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you remember the name of the Minister of Interior, again with reference to that particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not quite sure -- I think it was Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You said a couple of hours ago that the Government had "no control" -- I am quoting what you said -- "no control over armed formations". Did the Government have any enforcement agency at its disposal -- we are speaking of course of the Government of the district of -- the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I meant to ask you whether the Government had any police force -- any military units under its control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the Government could not have any influence over any police or military units in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What were the links or the relations between the Government and the JNA, or paramilitary units in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I do not know anything about any paramilitary formations. The army was there and the Territorial Defence was there. The Territorial Defence of course was part of the armed forces. As for the paramilitary units, I do not know what the definition is, nor did we as a Government have any formations in this respect. As far as the army is concerned, in the southern part, from Sid onwards to Vukovar, we had no links with them, and as for this part where the seat of the Government was, we had only links as much as we had to ask for permits for movement or to carry out any work in the field -- farming work -- and, also, depending on the competencies of the Ministries, that was the only touch that we had with them. Although we as a Government, as far as I am able to remember, we were not happy, because we had to do that, because, in some areas, we would be checked every 100 metres if we moved through some areas and we often lodged protests with the military administration -- I do not know what all those departments were in the army -- the logistics and so on -- to do something. I can give you an example from my jurisdiction. Since there were no telephone links, if there was a man, a professional man who was supposed to do something about it, there was this whole procedure that had to be gone through in order to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But did you hold consultations -- did the Government hold consultations with the army -- with the military commanders or with the commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the Government as a whole. At the Government sessions, some information would filter through, but I as a Minister, and most of the other Ministers, we did not participate in that -- whether somebody in the Government had that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you please explain to me the following: I am reading the minutes, document D53, the exhibit produced by the Defence. These are the minutes of the meeting in Erdut on 19 November 1991. In point 2, item 2, it is stated, and I will read slowly -- actually, I wonder whether the witness could be given a copy of the Serbian version, so that he can follow in the original text -- it is D53. It is item 2, it is stated here and I will read slowly: "Goran Hadzic, President of the Government, briefed those present ..." including yourself: " ... about the current situation from the international point of view and the talks which had been held with the representatives of the Republic of Serbia and the Yugoslav People's Army. Radovan Stojcic briefed those present on the military situation. The following took part in the discussion." And a few names follow. Then it is stated, and I quote: "A unanimous decision was reached that the commander of the Territorial Defence had their full confidence and that his status had been established by the decision of the Great People's Assembly which proclaimed that units of the Territorial Defence form a part of the Yugoslav forces." If you move to the following page on the English version, it is stated, and again I quote: "The following conclusions were unanimously adopted." If you skip number 1 and 2, you read number 3: "That a joint meeting of representatives of the Republic of Serbia and the JNA shall be organised, that a joint meeting with representatives of other Serbian districts that will be organised." And 5: "That JNA units are subordinated to the Government of the Serbian district on its territory." Could you please help us by explaining the meaning of this particular decision, "JNA units are subordinated to the Government of the Serbian district on its territory", because reading a simple reading from outside of these minutes would convey the idea that there were close links between the JNA and the Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, such decisions, as I already said, are the result of the fact that there were so few links and all the problems that I have described, how it was difficult for us to move around this territory, so this was the result -- this was the conclusion, so that the JNA recognises the Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me give you a clarification, I apologise for interrupting the witness and the court. In the Serbian version it says that the Serbian Government "shall be" or "will be" -- that is the future in Serbian and in paragraph 5 of the English translation, there is the present tense, so we have to make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the witness could read, in Serbian, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just explain about paragraph 3. It says, "organises a joint meeting with the representatives of the Republic of Serbia and JNA" -- that was precisely for those reasons, because there were no communications and Serbia was mentioned here in order to maybe exert some influence over the JNA so that this meeting would take place, and paragraph 5 was that it "will be" or "shall be" above, or subordinate to the JNA units, which means that at the time it had no influence over those units, so this was an intention, an ambition of the Government. Of course, this never took place, because the Government itself did not have a long mandate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you explain the fact that under item 2 it is stated that: "The President of the Government briefed the other members of the Government about the current situation and the relations with the JNA and Radovan Stojcic briefed those present on the military situation."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was just information that we received from other members -- mostly from the Prime Minister -- and we, other members of the Government, could only talk about this information -- those pieces of information, but we could not take part in the decision-making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the issues of personnel are concerned, with regard to the Territorial Defence, the Government had no influence over who was to be a commander of the Territorial Defence, but, in one of the decrees, it is obvious that it was a good thing, but it only has to do with certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether Mr. Jovan Pejakovic was present at the meeting of the Government on the 20th in VELEPROMET, namely, the clerk of the Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jovan Pejakovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: He was the man who wrote the minutes of the meeting held by the Government on 19 November 1991 in Erdut. I was wondering whether the same clerk was also present -- officer, registrar -- present at the meeting of the Government that took place on 20 November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether Jovan Jakovic was present at this meeting, but I do know that he signed the minutes of the Government meetings, which does not mean that he attended all those meetings of the Government, because there was also somebody who acted as the recording clerk and then he would sign it as the efficient recording clerk. I cannot remember whether he was there on 20 November. Most of the members of the Government arrived in a single vehicle, except for myself -- I went there in my own car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether anybody was there to take minutes -- to record the main points of the discussion on 20 November -- whether or not thereafter minutes were produced, whether somebody was taking notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember that anyone took any form of notes, or took down the minutes and if there had been somebody from the Government making the minutes, I would have seen it. I have not seen it, so I assume that nobody took down the notes, but we did not even have the agenda -- I remember that clearly. It was not a usual meeting of the Government -- it was a meeting of the members of the Government and some five or six other people -- I do not know who they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In a way it was rather unusual, first of all, because there was no agenda and, secondly, because it was held one day after the other meeting -- normally governments do not meet every day -- and, thirdly, no minutes were taken. How do you explain the unusual character or nature of this meeting of the Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will give you an explanation of what preceded the arrival of the members of the Government to Vukovar. The atmosphere was such that it was not necessary for the Government to go to Vukovar and actually the attitude was if the Government came to Vukovar at all, that maybe something could happen, maybe even a conflict. They could even be banned from entering Vukovar. The conclusion at the previous meeting was that we should go, but each of us had to make our own personal decision whether we would go there, considering all the risks, and considering the aversion towards this Government that prevailed in the town itself. Once we were there and once we saw what the situation was, it was impossible to set up the agenda and to hold a meeting of the Government, which would result in some conclusions. In such an atmosphere, it was simply -- we were all very surprised by what we saw there, and we did hold the meeting and the Government felt that the aim had been achieved and that it was clear that the Government existed in Vukovar, that it had not been destroyed, so that was the only contribution -- maybe that is not a good term. That was some kind of progress for that Government, that it was able to appear to be in Vukovar, in a town in which it had -- with which it had nothing to do until that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Two minor questions. We saw previously a videotape and we saw many, many people, including Mr. Dokmanovic and other well-known persons, such as Arkan. Those people there were before the meeting -- what we saw on the videotape, did it happen before the meeting of the Government, or after the meeting of the Government? I am not clear about this -- those people who were gathered there, all together, were they there before they started the meeting of the Government or were they there after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what video you saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The one we saw before in court, when it was shown to you at the request of Defence counsel, to identify Mr. Dokmanovic -- it was in black and white and not in colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is probably before the meeting of the Government when people had already arrived, because, after the meeting, everybody went their own way. I think that after the meeting they did not linger in the VELEPROMET compound -- at least, I did not -- I just stayed there for about five minutes and then went straight to my car and left and since there are quite a few people in that video, it could have been only before the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Did Arkan take part in the meeting of the Government, since he was there, you said, probably as a sort of chief of security of the Prime Minister, so I was wondering whether he took part in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Arkan did not take part in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: One final question, which has nothing to do with the issue we have been discussing. You were born in Slavonia, in the Republic of Croatia -- you were born in Pacetin. In this period which we are now discussing, between September and December 1991, were you a citizen of Croatia -- what citizenship did you have in that particular period, leaving aside nationality and ethic origin, this is of no importance to us; what was your citizenship in this period between September and December 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Vinkovci. I lived in Pacetin -- I had the ID card that was issued in Vukovar, and at the time none of us thought about our citizenship. We all thought that we had Yugoslav citizenship, and I felt that I was a citizen of Yugoslavia, despite the fact that you had republics within the federation, but the citizenship was Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I know, but we were told by the Defence counsel that in addition to the Yugoslav citizenship, every person also had citizenship of a particular republic -- the republic where he was born or where he was living. I assume you had the citizenship of Croatia in addition to the citizenship of Yugoslavia; is that correct, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. In some of the documents in the birth certificates and so forth, in addition to the Yugoslav citizenship, in some cases, it is stated that there was the citizenship of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And so you held this citizenship also of the Republic of Croatia also in the period between September and December when you were a member of the Government of the district?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I am asking this question for a particular legal reason, because we were told in court that there was a provision in one of the laws passed by the Assembly of the Government [sic] of the Serbian district, whereby the citizenship of Croatia was annulled -- was made invalid and only the citizenship of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was retained by living in this area. Am I correct in saying that probably you did not attach any importance to this particular provision about the withdrawal of the republican citizenship, for those living in the territory under the control and the authority and the jurisdiction of the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you are right, but if I can make a clarification, this may be a decision passed by the Assembly -- I cannot recall what the decision was that was made by the Assembly, but I do know that the Republic of Serbia and Krajina, or rather the Serbian district, never reached the stage in which it would issue certificates of citizenship of the Serbian State. It never happened in the Republic of Serbia and Krajina. The only thing was that we were issued with ID cards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether there are any further questions arising out of those questions which I have put. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have just one note -- when you asked the question, the last question, you said it was the decision of the Government. It was not the decision of the Government but of the assembly -- the decision on citizenship, so I would like that to be corrected in the transcript -- that is why he is not aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Who said the decision of the Government, the witness or -- because I am aware -- I know probably it was a mistake, but I am fully aware that the law I was quoting, I think it was article 4 -- I am quoting by heart, was a law passed by the Assembly of the Serbian district. There is no doubt about that -- not by the Government. I know that the Government could not pass laws. Are there any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Just one formal matter. For Witness DA, we have not filed an official request for him to be named under this pseudonym, so I hereby request permission for this witness to be named as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We had already granted the request of course, and this applies also, I assume, to the next witnesses, yes? There is no problem about that. There is therefore no objection to Witness DA being released? I would like to thank you so much, Witness DA, for coming here to give evidence in court and you may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would also like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next witness, your Honours, I do not know what the reason is, and it is not up to me to think about the reasons why you asked the questions that you did ask of this witness, but let me clarify something. In the pre-trial brief, the Defence counsel submitted documents about this Government, about the Ministries, and the Ministers. This has not been admitted into evidence, but the Registry has that document and it has been translated into English. So, if you need that, it should not be a problem for the Registrar to have those documents brought into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Fila, I thank you. Of course, you know very well that there is a huge difference -- very often in our countries there is a huge difference between the law and the reality. We are interested in what happened in reality -- not only in the normative --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is not what I wanted to say. I just wanted to make it clear to you that you have that document at your disposal. I just wanted to be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. I suggest that we move on with your next witness, and then we take a break around, say, 10 to 12. Is that suitable? The next witness will be DB?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I move that he be named DB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Witness DB, may I ask you to be so kind as to make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may be seated. WITNESS DB

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I should like the witness to be shown this piece of paper with his name on it to confirm that he is that individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name and surname.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D54, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should like to ask that we enable a member of my team with the tape to come in. He is an investigator of the Defence, but the security men will not let him pass, and he has the tape which we are going to play and our witness is on the tape. Could you ask them to let him in, please? Thank you. Otherwise, we would have technical problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would the Witness DB be shown the document that I have in my hands in the Serbian and English translations, and tell us whether that is the statement he gave to the Defence investigator, that is to say, in the English translation. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D55, English translation D55A, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If there are no remarks, I propose that this document be tendered and admitted as D55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness DB, did you graduate from the faculty of economics in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Vukovar, I was born in Vukovar and lived in Vukovar the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was employed in Vukovar. I held several jobs. Shall I enumerate them? At the beginning, I worked in the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar and, later on, in the waterworks of the city of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long did you live in Vukovar and when did you leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Vukovar up until 22 July 1991, when I left the town because I felt unsafe there. I felt that life in Vukovar was unsafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you feel, the fact that it was unsafe -- did you have any adverse experiences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this lack of security was reflected in some of the incidents that took place previously, and there was some cafes that were blown up, the proprietors of which were Serbs. After that, several prominent citizens disappeared -- Serbs, again. Let me mention the name of Mladen Mrkic -- he was one of them. The others I cannot recall at the present time, but there were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you mobilised by the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was mobilised by the Yugoslav People's Army, and I can say that it was at the beginning of September and on the occasion I was given duties, I was to see to the chemical and hygienic control of the drinking water of the town and to organise water supplies in the rural settlements where this was a possibility, given the technical facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did the waterworks supply function in Vukovar and the surrounding villages in the period that we are talking about, that is to say, from the autumn of 1991 to the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that period, there was no organised water supply system. In the city of Vukovar itself, the population got its water supplies from open sources -- open water sources -- water wells, and, at that time, I conducted the analysis of the water that I spoke to you about a moment ago and in the rural areas, where for technical reasons this was possible, we set up power generators for the production of electricity, which were put into motion by pumps, and in shorter periods of time, during the day, there was a certain amount of water. There were some water supplies in the villages, but it was just enough for people to come and collect the water they needed for their daily needs, either for drinking or to prepare food -- for cooking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since when have you known Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have known Slavko Dokmanovic since the time I began working in the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar and about two years -- we worked two years in the same office, for about two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did Dokmanovic become the President of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dokmanovic became President of the Municipal Assembly after the first multi-Party elections in Croatia, which means some time in the spring -- April or May of 1990. I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long did he perform his functions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The function of President of the Municipal Assembly, according to my knowledge, he performed until the end of May and the beginning of June, more or less, 1991, when he was incapacitated from further carrying out that function.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any direct knowledge as to when and how he was prevented from coming to the Municipal Assembly building to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my direct knowledge is the following: on one particular day, I cannot exactly remember the date, Slavko Dokmanovic was in my family home, when he was informed that he would not be able to leave Vukovar safely in the direction of Trpinja and Slavko Dokmanovic then called the commander of the barracks and requested a military vehicle -- an armoured military vehicle -- which then took him to Trpinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On 20 November, were you in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Vukovar on 20 November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How do you recall that it was precisely 20 November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I remember because I was in Vukovar on 19 November as well, because my wife and I went to look for her mother, who spent the entire time in Vukovar, and on that particular day, 19 November, we found my mother-in-law, and on 19 November, we took her in the direction of Sid, where the rest of her family was located, which means the father and the brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On 20 November, where were you in Vukovar exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, on 20 November, in the building of VELEPROMET and my wife and I, because on 19 November we did not find my aunt, which was the only member of my family who had remained, so we went to look for her on 20 November, and, for that particular reason, in the early hours of 20 November, we returned to Vukovar. We were in the VELEPROMET compound, because that was the place where all the civilian population was gathered -- all the population leaving the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you thought that you would find the individuals who you were looking for there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I hoped to find my aunt there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I should like the witness to be shown a segment of the tape from D2 -- Exhibit D2, does he recognise any of the individuals, does he recognise himself on the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You need not identify yourself, just the other people you recognise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Mr. Jovan Cvetkovic, Goran Hadzic, this is Dusan Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we replay the tape from the beginning? Perhaps he will recognise somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rade Leskovac, Nebojsa Lazarevic, Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the defendant anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can now see the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you show the witness photographs -- stills -- taken from this segment of the tape, so that he can identify himself without indicating publicly who he is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D56.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you show him this still as well -- show the witness the following still? (Handed). Are the stills what you saw on the tape a moment ago, and do you recognise yourself on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is I.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were at the VELEPROMET compound on that day, 20 November, when that tape was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Slavko Dokmanovic on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing -- I can describe it as a hunting suit -- a hunting uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The second photograph is marked D57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the second photograph -- I am not following -- what is D57?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The second photograph is also a photograph taken from the videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it supposed to show?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand corner, you can see Witness DB, on the left-hand side, whereas, up front is somebody else -- I do not know if the witness recognises that individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So, on the left-hand side is the image, the picture, of our Witness DB. I should like Witness DB to be shown Defence exhibit number 48 -- D48, so that he can identify what Slavko Dokmanovic was wearing on that particular occasion and whether it is the suit that he most frequently wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May we continue? Do you know whether, on that day, 20 November, a meeting of the Government members was held in the VELEPROMET compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there was a meeting of some kind being held -- it is possible that it was a meeting of the Government, but I did not know that at the time, but I know that there was a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that there was a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of the meeting, I stayed outside the doors of the building and talked to some other people who did not attend the meeting. We talked about many things, because those people were my friends and acquaintances, and I had not seen them for three or four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the courtyard of the VELEPROMET building and where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in the courtyard of VELEPROMET -- we stayed there until about half past 3 -- 3.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, we went in the direction of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who were you with, but do not mention their names, please, and where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was with my wife, and my own personal car, in a column, with the other people who were present on the occasion, and we went towards -- in the direction of Negoslavci, Orolik and Sid, where my wife's family was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you stop along the way, on the road from VELEPROMET towards Sid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were several stops -- the first stop, as far as I recall, was in Negoslavci, there was a control of some kind -- a check of some kind -- I do not know what, because it was a long column of vehicles and we did not see why we were being stopped, but we were stopped for a short period of time. After that, we moved in the direction of the Orolik village, where at the entry to the village we were stopped. In front of us there was a column of buses -- a long line of buses, and we remained there for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what time of the day this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As it was winter time, it was around dusk -- night had begun to fall -- somewhere around 4 or half past five in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before getting to Orolik, did you notice a crowd in which Slavko Dokmanovic was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a sort of crowd, but it was a situation in which visibility was reduced, so I could not ascertain who was in the crowd and why the incident had taken place -- what was happening exactly, but when I moved closer, because I did not stay in my car, I heard that Slavko Dokmanovic had taken part in that general commotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And then you passed the buses and continued along your way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after that incident, traffic was allowed again -- vehicles could move forward, whereas the buses remained where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that same day, where did you last see Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him for the last time in front of Orolik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what the general situation looked like -- it was winter time, as I say -- it was around 5 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was in control of the town immediately after its liberation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was military rule -- the town was administered by military rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to show the witness a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you whether you have many other questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We can then decide when to take a recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I will complete my examination-in-chief in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D58 and the English translation D58A. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of document is this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document by which the military command appoints me the head of the waterworks, with the task of first and foremost retaining the waterworks property.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you read out the document, please, where it says "I order" and below that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). The provisional administrator is given these competencies to protect the property, which has been given to him to administer. In taking over his duties, he is duty-bound to set up a commission to determine the state of the property and the equipment, to make a list of the situation as found and to determine whether the equipment or property has been damaged in any way. He is also duty-bound to list any changes that take place and to inform the command thereof. It is prohibited to alienate any property or equipment from the former waterworks without the knowledge and go-ahead of this command. The provisional manager may engage a minimum number of workers, according to their qualification structure, necessary to maintain the equipment and property for use. This command should be supplied with a list of the workers engaged in order for them to be given permits."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is the signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commander -- Colonel Milorad Vojnovic and the stamp says the "military post number 77 of Kragujevac".

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The commander of what place -- what locality -- what town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why the commander -- why does the commander of the town appoint a manager for the waterworks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because, at that period, as I said, the town was administered by military rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions. I should just like to ask the redaction and the evidence that we have been tendered be admitted under the numbers we have submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We take a 20-minute recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, you said in your evidence that you had a position in the municipality prior to the war; do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You misunderstood me. I worked as a clerk in the municipality -- I did not hold a function there -- I was not an official of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long had you worked there -- I think that -- I gathered from your evidence that you drew a distinction from working in the municipality and the position you had in the waterworks, or are you saying that they were both the same position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, let me explain. From 1979 until 1984, I worked in the municipality as a clerk, in the administrative department, so I did not have a post -- a function there. After 1984 -- November 1984 -- I worked in the waterworks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You worked in the waterworks right up until the beginning of the war, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you knew Mr. Dokmanovic rather well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that -- we were friends -- quite close friends -- we visited each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think the two families were friends -- your family and Mr. Dokmanovic's family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the war -- and I am talking about the period August through to November of 1991 -- what work did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said that I was assigned by the JNA to carry out the chemical and bacteriological control of the drinking water.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You worked under Mr. Dokmanovic during this period -- that is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- I was given my tasks by the army -- I received orders from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was not asking you who gave you the tasks; I am merely saying that did you not work either for or with Mr. Dokmanovic during this period, because he was in the position of the Minister for Agriculture in the Government of the Serbian district of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem and because his duties included water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so you saw him during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times -- actually, maybe two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The position that you had, even though you were assigned -- the position you had during this period that you were assigned by the military authorities, was that a military position, or a civilian position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a military position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout the time that I carried out my function, my tasks, actually, I had people with me who escorted me and who drove me to the places where I had to carry out my duties, so there was no need for me to carry weapons. My job, my function, did not call for weapons to be carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But nevertheless you wore a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the type of uniform that you wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was a camouflage uniform -- a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did it have insignia or markings on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, since I did not hold a rank in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you wear a military cap or hat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not wear a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you get the uniform from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received the uniform in Sid. I cannot remember -- it was a building where I was issued this uniform and assigned to carry out those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And this was a military establishment, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: People who were not necessarily performing military duties such as yourself often wore military uniforms, did they not, so people performing civilian functions, if I could call it that, during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Among other things, I also wore the military uniform when it was not necessary, and the reason for that was because I did not have other clothes, because all my clothes remained in the house to which I had not access during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In fact, it is true, is it not, that from time to time members of the Government of the Serbian district of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem wore uniforms of a sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, because I did not meet with the members of the Government often.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We saw the video a moment ago, Exhibit D2, and in that we see, or we saw Goran Hadzic -- do you remember pointing him out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He was at the time walking or with Arkan -- do you remember seeing that in the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember seeing Goran Hadzic. I did not know Arkan at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I was to tell you that the gentleman that was walking beside him was Arkan, can you tell me why Mr. Hadzic -- Goran Hadzic was dressed in the same uniform as Arkan, or maybe you do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You know Goran Hadzic, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Goran Hadzic from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, during that time, that is, November 1991, what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know from the media, from the press, that he was the Prime Minister in the Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And he was wearing a military uniform at the time -- you agree with that -- in the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose so. I cannot confirm that with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to be precise about it, so I will ask the video D2 be played again and you can look at it yourself and we can point it out -- you can point out Mr. Goran Hadzic for me, please. I do not know that it is possible for it to be played now, but I can move on and come back, if that is necessary. Just look at this video as it is played. The moment you see Goran Hadzic, I will ask that the video be stopped -- the frame be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can we scroll back and I will ask the video to be stopped. I wanted you to say and we will stop at that point. If we can roll more forward now, a couple more frames?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Those two gentlemen, they appear to be dressed in the same uniform, do they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one could say that on the basis of this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Looking at the screen -- directly at the screen -- the person on the right side, do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot say that I met Arkan, but I saw his face later on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Arkan is the gentleman on the left-hand side looking at the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the gentleman immediately beside him is Goran Hadzic, the Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know this military uniform -- can you recognise the military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know this uniform -- the army that I dealt with, they did not wear uniforms like these.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly not a JNA uniform -- you would agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I want to move on, if I may, to the events that occurred on 20 November 1991, or immediately just prior to that -- I think you said that you went to Vukovar first on 19 November and then again on 20 November -- I think that was your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the 19th, where did you leave from when you went there on the 19th -- where did you go from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, on the 20th, where did you leave from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also from Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am just wondering if you could help us by showing us on a map the route that you followed. I would ask the witness be shown Exhibit P4. I am wondering if you would do something for me. I will have the map put on the screen there beside you. It will appear on your television set but I would ask you to look at it on the machine beside you, to your right. Just with a pointer, could you show us firstly where Sid is? It has to come up on the screen -- yes, okay. Just take your time and orient yourself and when you feel comfortable with the map, see if you can find Sid for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness points on the map) the route went as follows -- to Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you mention the towns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Tovarnik, Ilaca, Sidski Banovci, Orolik, then you go past Berak, but not through Berak, Negoslavci, Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that the route that you followed on both days -- 19 and 20 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. That is the only route one could take towards Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that the only route because it was the only route open or because it was the only way you could get there by car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was the only route that was open in the direction of Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Coming back on the 19th, what route did you follow then -- coming back from Vukovar to Sid on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same route.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same route.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The route from Vukovar to Sid, on the way that you have shown, goes past a turnoff which goes off to Ovcara farm, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On 20 November 1991, what time did you arrive at VELEPROMET, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may have been around 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, when you arrived there, did you go anywhere else, or did you just stay at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only in the VELEPROMET building, since that was the place where the civilian population congregated and that was the place where I expected to find my aunt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Dokmanovic arrive at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What time did he arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He arrived at around 2 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was he with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was with Rade Leskovac, Goran Hadzic, Jovan Cvetkovic, Nebojsa Lazarevic and a group of people whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you see the car that he arrived in -- assuming he came by car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not see the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you talk to Mr. Dokmanovic on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was just the usual chit-chat; how are you, how is your family, is everyone alive and well, do you have any problems -- things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that, after Mr. Dokmanovic -- I withdraw that. I think you said that there was a meeting of the Government at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, I knew that there was some kind of a meeting going on, but I did not know that that was the meeting of the Government. After that, after the fact, I heard from other people that it was the meeting of the Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who participated in the meeting? I know you did not go in and see it yourself, but did you know who went into the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- I remained in front of the building, talking to the people who had also remained in front of the building. I do not know who entered into the building to attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what time the meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know how long it lasted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember now, maybe about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You saw Mr. Dokmanovic when he first arrived and you think that was about 2 o'clock. The meeting then followed after that, did it -- is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Dokmanovic again in VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Dokmanovic after he had left the VELEPROMET building -- in that area where I stood at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was outside the building, in the yard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You obviously did not see him when he attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The time that you saw him after, did you speak to him then, or did you just see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just saw him -- we did not talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you keep him under observation for -- how long did you look at him for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, maybe about 10 minutes -- it was a joint agreement that we should all set off in a line of vehicles towards Sid because we were all going in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who proposed this joint agreement -- who said this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember. It has been a long time, so I do not remember who it was, who said that -- who proposed this, but we did reach an agreement, although I do not know who initiated the agreement -- I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many cars were there at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I was at the beginning of the line of vehicles, I cannot really say -- maybe about 10 vehicles, maybe even more -- I cannot say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any trucks or buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that column, there were only cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say you set off, you were in the front of the column -- did you remain in the front of the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that I was the first car, but I was in the front among the very first vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who were in the vehicles ahead of you or behind you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, all those people who were there when this agreement was reached that we should all set off in a column of vehicles -- that means it was Goran Hadzic, Leskovac, Slavko Dokmanovic, Lazarevic, Cvetkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You went directly from VELEPROMET to Negoslavci, did you, or did you stop on the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went directly from VELEPROMET in the direction of Negoslavci and then we stopped for a short period in Negoslavci. The reason was because there was a line, or a checkpoint in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You did not stop at Ovcara on the way through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This route does not lead via Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you can get to Ovcara off this route, can you not, by turning off the road and going --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, from the route, but we did not stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you left VELEPROMET, the next time you saw Slavko Dokmanovic was at Orolik, I think you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did -- actually, yes, I am sorry, I misunderstood your question -- yes -- not in Orolik, but outside of the village of Orolik, we stopped because there was a line of buses. That is when I saw Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were working in the Municipal Assembly, did you know a person called Emil Cukalovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that you said that, when you were in VELEPROMET, you stayed in the compound all the time -- did you not say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it not true that you went over to the JNA barracks, which was nearby VELEPROMET, during that day of 20 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no need for me to go there, because no civilian population was gathered there, according to the information at my disposal at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You were looking for your aunt, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it not true that you went to the JNA barracks and there were a number of buses with people loaded in them -- in the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the courtyard of VELEPROMET there were a number of buses with people on them. I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am talking about JNA barracks, which is very nearby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it not true that you walked around these buses and that you saw, among other people there, Emil Cukalovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did walk around the buses, but I cannot recall -- I saw many people whom I knew. It is possible that I saw Emil Cukalovic there, too, but I cannot recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These people had been brought there from the Vukovar hospital, had they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I put it to you that, at the time, you knew full well that the people on those buses were going to be taken to Ovcara, where they were going to be liquidated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I put it to you that the people that had gathered at VELEPROMET knew that this is what was going to happen to those people who were kept in the buses at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should like to ask to restrict ourselves to asking the witness questions -- not to intimidate the witnesses. I am interested in Mr. Niemann's questions -- they are important -- not his assertions there was a group of buses. A question is being asked by Mr. Niemann and the other the witness is asking. If you look at the transcript, you will see this, and it would be a good idea to clarify that up -- whether we are dealing with the group of buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is entirely appropriate for me to put propositions to the witness in circumstances such as this, your Honour, bearing in mind the testimony that has been called in this case -- entirely appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I think Mr. Niemann is right. He asked questions of the witness and the witness said "no" and so it is a different way of putting questions, which is appropriate, because these questions were based on the testimony of another witness. Do you have any questions for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just the question of the buses. What group of buses were you talking about? Can we clarify the group of buses in question? It is not clear from what has been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are you asking this question of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, what buses has the witness in mind when he says he saw them -- where did he see those buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the buses in front of Orolik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, with the group of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In VELEPROMET.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor is asking or asked you whether you were at the barracks and whether you saw buses at the barracks with people in them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said no, and my answer was no to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It was very clear also to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, your Honour, just two questions to clarify matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The question asked by the Prosecutor as to whether the position held in autumn was a military one and you said "Yes"; would you tell us whether the position you were placed at was a civilian post, or whether the -- to which the military command had appointed you was a civilian post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I was appointed to by the military command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May we clarify another matter? Did you see Dokmanovic coming and who did he come with, and you mentioned Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that Mr. Dokmanovic had come with Mr. Hadzic or did you say that Mr. Hadzic -- that Mr. Dokmanovic was there in the group with Mr. Hadzic, so he had not come with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that -- I cannot say who came with whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No questions? I assume there is no objection to the witness being released. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may be released. I wonder whether Mr. Fila or Mr. Petrovic could tell us whether they need a lot of time for -- is it too late? Do you prefer to adjourn now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I fear that it would be best to begin tomorrow morning. We have one more witness that we have called for this part of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should like to ask something as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I wanted to ask something but the witness does not have to hear it. I would like to ask your Honours to allow me to say something. The witness that is coming tomorrow, and it is the wife of the previous witness -- we have concluded our list of witnesses -- when the Prosecutor presented his evidence, witness Vidic mentioned that Mr. Dokmanovic took part in a mission -- in a broadcast by Television Novi Sad and that they did not like it. The book that Mr. Williamson has been showing persistently, with a National Council of some kind -- I do not know what it is about -- the author is a certain Petrovic. The tape that I have in my possession has three-fold importance: first, it is the programme mentioned; second, the programme shows that Dokmanovic was not a member of the Serbian People's Council, and I am sorry to disappoint the Prosecutor, but that is evident on the tape and, thirdly, we hear the attitude of Mr. Dokmanovic with regard to extremists and non-extremists. It is a tape taken in the spring of 1991. If the court agrees, we can show the tape tomorrow -- I would like to give it to the interpreters -- to prepare it, because it lasts for two hours, but I said that it has three-fold importance. It is important on three counts -- first of all, to hear what Dokmanovic says and to hear what the individual who is a member of the Serbian National Council says. Fourthly, in the supporting material provided by the Prosecutor it is stated that Dokmanovic in that particular programme said that the Croats were not a mature nation, which must be placed under political tutelage. On this tape we can see that Mr. Dokmanovic never said those words, but the author of the book did -- of that capital work that the Prosecutor constantly is placing before the Tribunal. So, if you agree, I should like to show this tape tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not know what the tape is, and I find it objectionable that we get a summary of evidence of what its contents are in this way. The tape speaks for itself. If there is a tape, which I have no idea what it is, if it is of any benefit to the Defence, they should present it in the usual way as an exhibit and we can deal with it in that way. But I cannot respond to something that has been said. I had heard at one stage -- I think Mr. Fila suggested playing the BBC programme -- "The Death of Yugoslavia". I do not know that this is the tape he is talking about, but I have some views and comments on that, if that is what he is talking about. That is something I have seen. I do not know whether or not this is the same one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "The Death of Yugoslavia", I think we agreed that this tape should be shown, but it is the Prosecution that has the tape, not myself, and I think it would be beneficial for us to see that tape, if that is what Mr. Niemann is talking about. This tape is by Television Novi Sad, and Mr. Dokmanovic takes part as the President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar. You can see it tomorrow. I shall be tendering it in evidence, of course. But I do not have any abridged version, neither did I receive any abridged versions from the Prosecution, which I have looked through. So, when people are leaving Vukovar, the Jewish choir is singing -- that is probably the abridged version of something longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not know what Mr. Fila is talking about -- unless it is a video that we have provided, I do not know what the video is about and I can only suggest that, if he can give us a copy of it, we can look at it overnight and would be in a much better position to respond to it in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I wonder whether you could give a copy to the interpreters and to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have just one example -- they can copy it as much as they like, but I have only this one example and do not have the possibilities of technically multiplying this. Take a look at it and we can play it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Give a copy maybe to the Registry for the interpreters and for the Prosecutor -- the Prosecutor I hope will be able to make a copy. I wonder whether we could receive from either party as soon as possible a still of the accused, of Mr. Goran Hadzic and Mr. Arkan taken from the videotape we saw today, as well as other videotapes. In particular this applies to the accused, whether we could have a still of the various pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will do that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In colour, if possible -- not in black and white. You may remember that tomorrow we start at 8.30 and we sit on another case, so we will resume on the case of Mr. Dokmanovic at 10 o'clock sharp. We stand adjourned now. (At 1 p.m. the matter adjourned until Wednesday, 29th April 1998 at 10 a.m.)
